title: Portugal's housing marches, America's measles setback and grounded flights

stories.headline: Tens of thousands march across Portugal over soaring housing costs
stories.headlineZh: 葡萄牙数万人上街游行，抗议住房成本飙升
stories.summaryZh: 葡萄牙30多个城镇爆发全国性住房抗议，民众要求限制租金上涨、加强租户保护。
stories.c1:
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of more than 30 Portuguese towns and cities on Saturday, in what organisers described as the largest nationwide demonstration since their housing movement emerged only weeks ago. Marchers in Lisbon, Porto, Faro, Coimbra and Braga, ranging from teenagers to retirees, rallied under the banner of Casa Para Viver, or "A Home to Live In", a coalition of roughly 100 housing associations and grassroots groups.

Their grievances are rooted in a dramatic surge in costs. According to Eurostat, Portugal recorded the steepest rise in the European Union in house prices relative to incomes between 2015 and 2025, at 61 per cent, well ahead of the Netherlands in second place. The government acknowledges that rents have climbed 68 per cent since 2020, while property prices rose almost 20 per cent in the year to early 2026. Much of this has been attributed to foreign buyers and investment funds, as well as remote workers and retirees drawn by the mild coastal climate.

The immediate trigger, however, is legislation recently approved by parliament that makes rental contracts more flexible and speeds up evictions. Campaigners argue that the reforms will erode tenant protections at precisely the moment when housing is becoming scarcer. They are calling for caps on rent increases, stronger safeguards against eviction and tighter regulation of short-term tourist lets and vacant properties.

To be fair, the government has not been idle: it has cut taxes on new construction, restricted short-term rentals and pledged to build 145,000 homes, while conceding that the benefits will take time to materialise. Organisers have urged Prime Minister Luís Montenegro to meet them in person. The protests follow similar marches in neighbouring Spain in October, suggesting that housing may be becoming a defining issue for younger Europeans.
stories.b2:
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched in more than 30 towns and cities across Portugal. Organisers said it was the biggest national protest since their housing movement began a few weeks ago. People of all ages, from teenagers to retirees, joined marches in cities such as Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra. The protests were organised by Casa Para Viver, a group of about 100 housing organisations.

The main problem is cost. Eurostat figures show that between 2015 and 2025, house prices compared with incomes rose by 61 per cent in Portugal, the biggest increase in the EU. The government says rents have gone up 68 per cent since 2020. Foreign buyers, investment funds, remote workers and retirees are blamed for much of the rise.

The protests were also sparked by a new law passed by parliament. It makes rental contracts more flexible and makes evictions faster. Campaigners fear tenants will lose protection. They want limits on rent rises, more protection from eviction and stricter rules on holiday rentals and empty homes.

The government has lowered taxes on new buildings, limited short-term rentals and promised 145,000 new homes. However, it admits that these changes will take time. Similar protests happened in Spain in October.

vocab.en: to go out in public to protest
vocab.example: Students took to the streets to demand cheaper public transport.

vocab.en: organised by ordinary people rather than leaders
vocab.example: The campaign began as a small grassroots effort in one suburb.

vocab.en: to have its origin or cause in something
vocab.example: Her fear of dogs is rooted in a bad experience as a child.

vocab.en: to say that something is caused by something else
vocab.example: The doctor attributed his tiredness to stress and poor sleep.

vocab.en: an event that causes something to start
vocab.example: A small pay cut was the trigger for the strike.

vocab.en: to gradually weaken or reduce something
vocab.example: Constant broken promises can erode trust in a relationship.

vocab.en: a rule or measure that protects someone
vocab.example: The new app has strong safeguards to protect users' privacy.

vocab.en: to admit that something is true, often unwillingly
vocab.example: He conceded that his plan had a few weak points.

vocab.en: to actually happen or appear as expected
vocab.example: The promised pay rise never materialised.

questions.q: The protests took place in fewer than 30 towns and cities.
questions.explain: 原文说 "more than 30 Portuguese towns and cities"，与题干"少于30个"相矛盾，因此为 False。

questions.q: Prime Minister Luís Montenegro agreed to meet the organisers in person.
questions.explain: 原文只说组织者 "have urged Prime Minister Luís Montenegro to meet them in person"，没有提到总理是否同意，因此为 Not Given。

questions.q: According to Eurostat, the Netherlands had the second-largest rise in house prices relative to incomes in the EU.
questions.explain: 原文说 "well ahead of the Netherlands in second place"，说明荷兰排名第二，因此为 True。

questions.q: What does the article describe as the immediate trigger for the protests?
options: A sudden fall in the number of tourists
A 20 per cent rise in property taxes
A new law making rental contracts more flexible and evictions faster
The government's decision to stop building new homes
questions.explain: 原文说 "The immediate trigger... is legislation recently approved by parliament that makes rental contracts more flexible and speeds up evictions"，故选 C。

stories.discuss: Why do you think housing costs have become such a powerful issue for young people in many countries? What do you think governments should do first to make housing more affordable?

stories.headline: US loses measles-free status as cases more than double
stories.headlineZh: 病例翻倍，美国失去“消除麻疹”地位
stories.summaryZh: 泛美卫生组织取消美国的消除麻疹认证，今年确诊病例逾5400例，疫苗接种率持续下滑。
stories.c1:
The United States has lost its measles-free status, 26 years after the disease was declared eliminated there in 2000. The decision was made by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization's regional branch for the Americas, which revokes the status once measles has circulated without interruption for more than 12 months. Although Washington has withdrawn from the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO. The US thus joins Canada, Spain and the UK, all of which have recently been stripped of the same status.

More than 5,400 confirmed cases have been recorded so far this year, more than double the 2,289 reported in 2025. Two further deaths, in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, were announced on Friday, the latter involving an infant, bringing the number of measles-associated deaths this year to 10, according to Al Jazeera's count.

Even the death toll has become contested. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long cast doubt on the safety of the measles vaccine, asked the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to leave such deaths out of the official tally, arguing there was no evidence linking them to measles. Pennsylvania's governor, Josh Shapiro, has clashed with him over the issue, and epidemiologists point out that counting measles-associated deaths is long-standing practice.

Underlying the resurgence is a gradual slide in vaccination. Coverage among kindergarten children has fallen from 95.2 per cent in 2019-20 to 92.4 per cent, a seemingly modest drop that nonetheless leaves room for a highly contagious virus to spread. Two doses of the MMR vaccine offer about 97 per cent protection, and health departments have stepped up their vaccination efforts, but rebuilding public trust may prove far harder than restoring the numbers.
stories.b2:
The United States is no longer officially free of measles. The disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000. Now the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has removed this status because measles has spread continuously for more than a year. The US has left the World Health Organization, but it is still a member of PAHO. Canada, Spain and the UK have also lost the same status recently.

This year the US has recorded more than 5,400 confirmed cases, more than twice the number in 2025. On Friday, two more deaths were announced, one in Pennsylvania and one in Wisconsin. One of them was a baby. Al Jazeera counts 10 measles-related deaths in the US this year.

There is also an argument about the numbers. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has questioned the vaccine's safety for years, asked the CDC not to include these deaths in the official count. Pennsylvania's governor disagrees with him. Experts say counting such deaths is normal practice.

Fewer children are being vaccinated. Among kindergarten children, the rate has dropped from 95.2 per cent to 92.4 per cent. Two doses of the MMR vaccine give about 97 per cent protection, and health departments are working harder to encourage vaccination.

vocab.en: to officially take something away from someone
vocab.example: The athlete was stripped of his medal after failing a drug test.

vocab.en: argued about; not accepted by everyone
vocab.example: The results of the survey remain highly contested.

vocab.en: to make people less sure about something
vocab.example: New evidence has cast doubt on the witness's story.

vocab.en: to disagree strongly with someone
vocab.example: The coach often clashed with players over training methods.

vocab.en: having existed for a long time
vocab.example: The two companies have a long-standing partnership.

vocab.en: the return and growth of something after a decline
vocab.example: There has been a resurgence of interest in vinyl records.

vocab.en: to make something possible
vocab.example: The vague contract leaves room for misunderstanding.

vocab.en: spreading very easily from person to person
vocab.example: Chickenpox is highly contagious, so he stayed home from school.

vocab.en: to increase the amount or speed of an activity
vocab.example: Police have stepped up patrols around the stadium.

questions.q: PAHO removes measles-free status once the disease has spread continuously for more than 12 months.
questions.explain: 原文说 PAHO "revokes the status once measles has circulated without interruption for more than 12 months"，因此为 True。

questions.q: Most of this year's measles cases in the US involved unvaccinated adults.
questions.explain: 原文没有说明今年病例主要是哪类人群，因此为 Not Given。

questions.q: After leaving the WHO, the US also gave up its membership of PAHO.
questions.explain: 原文说 "Although Washington has withdrawn from the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO"，与题干矛盾，因此为 False。

questions.q: What has happened to vaccination coverage among US kindergarten children?
options: It has fallen from 95.2 per cent to 92.4 per cent
It has risen to about 97 per cent
It has dropped below 90 per cent for the first time
questions.explain: 原文说 "Coverage among kindergarten children has fallen from 95.2 per cent in 2019-20 to 92.4 per cent"，故选 A；97% 是两剂疫苗的保护率。

stories.discuss: Why do you think some people lose trust in vaccines even when diseases like measles return? How could health authorities rebuild that trust?

stories.headline: US flights grounded nationwide for over four hours after telecoms failure
stories.headlineZh: 通信故障致美国全国航班停飞逾四小时
stories.summaryZh: 美国空管通信系统故障，联邦航空局下令全国停飞，数千航班取消，官员称升级改造导致旧设备过载。
stories.c1:
Air travel across the United States was thrown into disarray on Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop, halting departures for more than four hours. The order was issued at 3:54pm Eastern Time after a telecommunications outage hit the centres that manage aircraft along air routes, and airspace was not reopened until 8:15pm. Planes already in the air were allowed to land, while international flights were dealt with case by case.

The knock-on effects were enormous. Data from FlightRadar24 showed that more than 4,700 flights were cancelled and around 10,000 delayed on Friday, with roughly 700 more cancellations for Saturday. By early evening, at least 827 flights had been diverted, most of them returning to the airports they had departed from. It was described as the longest ground stop in 25 years.

Ironically, the root cause appears to have been modernisation itself. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said switches and routers became overloaded with data and went down, and officials acknowledged that new technology being added to the system had overwhelmed older components, causing intermittent gaps in communications and radar. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ruled out a cyberattack. Critics note that a government report published in September had warned about ageing copper cables dating back to the 1960s and poorly scheduled upgrades.

Duffy insisted it was "safe to fly" but admitted that recovery would be slow, as airlines must reposition aircraft and crews across interconnected hubs. He expects normal operations to resume before the Thanksgiving travel peak and has called for $50 billion to upgrade air traffic control. Whether that money materialises, and whether contingency plans improve, will largely determine how resilient the system proves to be.
stories.b2:
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration stopped all flights from taking off across the United States for more than four hours. The order came at 3:54pm Eastern Time, after a telecommunications problem affected air traffic control centres. Airspace reopened at 8:15pm. Planes that were already flying were allowed to land.

The disruption was huge. According to FlightRadar24, more than 4,700 flights were cancelled and about 10,000 were delayed on Friday. Around 700 more flights were cancelled for Saturday. At least 827 flights were diverted. It was described as the longest ground stop in 25 years.

Officials said the problem was caused by new technology. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explained that switches and routers were overloaded with data and stopped working. The new equipment had put too much pressure on older parts of the system. Officials said it was not a cyberattack. A government report in September had already warned about old copper cables from the 1960s.

Duffy said flying was safe, but he admitted it would take time for airlines to recover. He expects normal operations before the busy Thanksgiving holiday and wants $50 billion to upgrade air traffic control.

vocab.en: to cause great confusion and disorder
vocab.example: The sudden storm threw the outdoor festival into disarray.

vocab.en: considering each situation separately
vocab.example: Requests for extra leave are decided case by case.

vocab.en: an indirect result of an event
vocab.example: The train strike had a knock-on effect on city traffic.

vocab.en: the basic reason why a problem happens
vocab.example: Poor communication was the root cause of the team's failure.

vocab.en: to be too much for something or someone to deal with
vocab.example: Thousands of orders overwhelmed the small online shop.

vocab.en: stopping and starting repeatedly
vocab.example: We had intermittent Wi-Fi all weekend.

vocab.en: to decide that something is not possible
vocab.example: Police have ruled out foul play in the incident.

vocab.en: a plan for what to do if something goes wrong
vocab.example: Every event needs a contingency plan in case it rains.

vocab.zh: 有韧性的；能迅速恢复的
vocab.en: able to recover quickly from problems
vocab.example: Small businesses proved surprisingly resilient during the downturn.

questions.q: A government report had warned about weaknesses in the system before the outage.
questions.explain: 原文说 "a government report published in September had warned about ageing copper cables... and poorly scheduled upgrades"，因此为 True。

questions.q: The ground stop lasted less than two hours.
questions.explain: 原文说 "halting departures for more than four hours"，与题干矛盾，因此为 False。

questions.q: Congress has already approved the $50 billion Duffy asked for.
questions.explain: 原文只说 Duffy "has called for $50 billion"，并未提及国会是否批准，因此为 Not Given。

questions.q: According to officials, what caused the outage?
options: A cyberattack on air traffic control
A severe storm damaging copper cables
A strike by air traffic controllers
New technology overloading older parts of the system
questions.explain: 原文说 "new technology being added to the system had overwhelmed older components"，且官员 "ruled out a cyberattack"，故选 D。

stories.discuss: Why do you think upgrading essential systems like air traffic control is so difficult? Should governments spend more on maintaining old infrastructure or on building new systems?

stories.headline: Queensland start-up says algae supplement cuts cattle methane by 65%
stories.headlineZh: 昆士兰初创公司称藻类饲料添加剂可减少牛甲烷排放65%
stories.summaryZh: 努萨一家公司用红藻制成低成本饲料添加剂，称可大幅减少牛打嗝排放的甲烷，但仍缺独立研究验证。
stories.c1:
A start-up based near Noosa on Queensland's Sunshine Coast believes it has found an affordable way to curb one of agriculture's most stubborn sources of emissions: the methane cattle release when they burp. Provectus Algae, founded eight years ago, grows red algae in a factory near Noosa and turns it into granular and liquid feed supplements for feedlots, dairy farms and grazing properties. The company claims its product cuts methane from burps by about 65 per cent.

The idea builds on a 2011 CSIRO finding that a native seaweed, Asparagopsis, could substantially reduce livestock methane. That approach ran into problems, however: a 2024 Murdoch University study found that cattle avoided feed containing high concentrations of the seaweed and showed signs of stomach ulcers and inflammation. Provectus replaced it with other algae and photosynthetic microbes, producing what chief executive Nusqe Spanton describes as a chemically similar product that targets methane-producing microbes without harming those that digest feed.

Pilot trials have involved more than 3,000 cattle, including at feedlots on the Darling Downs, and the Queensland government has contributed a $3.8 million grant to help bring the product to market. Spanton puts the average cost at about eight cents per animal per day. It is worth stressing, though, that these claims come from the company itself, and no independent peer-reviewed results were cited.

The stakes are considerable. CSIRO estimates that ruminant livestock account for more than 10 per cent of Australia's greenhouse gas emissions. University of Melbourne professor Richard Eckard says additives must cost less than 10 cents per animal per day to earn carbon-credit value, and that they work best in feedlots, where feed is eaten consistently. For the vast northern grazing sector, he argues, other solutions will still be needed.
stories.b2:
A company near Noosa in Queensland says it has found a cheap way to reduce the methane that cattle produce when they burp. Provectus Algae grows red algae in a factory and turns it into feed supplements for feedlots and farms. The company says its product reduces methane from burps by about 65 per cent.

The idea comes from a 2011 CSIRO discovery that a native seaweed called Asparagopsis could reduce methane from livestock. However, a 2024 study found that cattle avoided feed with a lot of this seaweed, and some had stomach problems. Provectus uses other algae and microbes instead. Its chief executive, Nusqe Spanton, says the product works in a similar way.

More than 3,000 cattle have been part of trials. The Queensland government has given the company a $3.8 million grant. The supplement costs about eight cents per animal per day. However, these results come from the company, not from independent research.

This matters because cattle and similar animals produce more than 10 per cent of Australia's greenhouse gas emissions. Professor Richard Eckard says the cost must stay under 10 cents a day. He also says additives work best in feedlots, so other solutions are needed for northern grazing land.

vocab.en: to control or limit something harmful
vocab.example: The city introduced new rules to curb noise at night.

vocab.en: difficult to remove, change or deal with
vocab.example: I've had a stubborn cough for weeks.

vocab.en: to use something as a base for further progress
vocab.example: This year's course builds on what you learnt last semester.

vocab.en: by a large amount
vocab.example: Online sales have increased substantially this year.

vocab.en: to start having difficulties
vocab.example: The project ran into problems when the funding was cut.

vocab.en: to start selling a new product
vocab.example: It took the team three years to bring the app to market.

vocab.en: used to emphasise an important point
vocab.example: It is worth stressing that the survey was very small.

vocab.en: a lot can be won or lost
vocab.example: With the final exam next week, the stakes are high for everyone.

vocab.en: to form a particular amount of something
vocab.example: Young people account for half of the app's users.

questions.q: The supplement has already been approved for export to overseas markets.
questions.explain: 原文没有提到出口或海外审批，因此为 Not Given。

questions.q: Provectus Algae's product is made from Asparagopsis seaweed.
questions.explain: 原文说 "Provectus replaced it with other algae and photosynthetic microbes"，即不再使用 Asparagopsis，因此为 False。

questions.q: The Queensland government has given the company financial support.
questions.explain: 原文说 "the Queensland government has contributed a $3.8 million grant"，因此为 True。

questions.q: According to Richard Eckard, where do feed additives work best?
options: In feedlots, where feed is eaten consistently
On dairy farms near the coast
questions.explain: 原文说 additives "work best in feedlots, where feed is eaten consistently"，故选 B。

stories.discuss: Do you think farmers should be required to reduce emissions from their animals, or should it be voluntary? Would you pay more for beef produced with lower emissions?

dialogue.title: A Jab Before the Trip
dialogue.setting: A university student visits her GP in Carlton to check her vaccinations before an overseas trip.
dialogue.settingZh: 一名大学生在卡尔顿的家庭医生诊所，出国前检查自己的疫苗接种情况。

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: Come on in, Mei, take a seat. So, what brings you in today?
lines.zh: 请进，梅，坐吧。今天来是有什么事？

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: I'm flying to the States next month, and I wanted to double-check my vaccinations.
lines.zh: 我下个月要飞去美国，想再确认一下我的疫苗接种情况。

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: Good thinking. Is there anything in particular that's got you worried?
lines.zh: 想得很周到。有什么特别让你担心的吗？

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Honestly, the measles stuff. I read this morning the US has lost its measles-free status.
lines.zh: 说实话，是麻疹的事。我今天早上看到美国失去了“无麻疹”地位。

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: Yeah, I saw that too. It's a bit of a wake-up call, to be fair.
lines.zh: 嗯，我也看到了。说实话，这确实算是个警钟。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: I had my jabs as a kid in Malaysia, but I've got no idea where the records are.
lines.zh: 我小时候在马来西亚打过疫苗，但完全不知道记录在哪儿。

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: No worries, that happens all the time. Let me pull up your history first.
lines.zh: 别担心，这种情况很常见。我先调出你的病历看看。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Would it be a problem if I just had another dose to be on the safe side?
lines.zh: 为了保险起见，我再打一针会有问题吗？

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: Not at all. If your records are unclear, an extra MMR dose is generally fine for adults.
lines.zh: 完全没问题。如果记录不清楚，成年人多打一剂麻腮风疫苗一般没关系。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: That's a relief. Does it need to be done a certain amount of time before I go?
lines.zh: 那我就放心了。需要在出发前多久打吗？

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: Ideally at least two weeks beforehand, so your body has time to build up protection.
lines.zh: 最好提前至少两周，这样身体有时间产生保护力。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Right, so I'd better not leave it till the last minute, then.
lines.zh: 明白了，那我最好别拖到最后一刻。

lines.name: Daniel
lines.en: Exactly. We can do it today if you're up for it. It's just a quick jab.
lines.zh: 没错。如果你愿意，今天就可以打。就一针，很快。

lines.name: Mei
lines.en: Let's get it over and done with, then. I'm not great with needles, mind you.
lines.zh: 那就赶紧打完吧。不过说真的，我挺怕打针的。

phrases.en: a bit of a wake-up call
to be on the safe side
leave it till the last minute
get it over and done with
